## Report: Reinhart & Rogoff, “Growth in a Time of Debt”

**1. The question, frozen.**  
I take the central question from the title and opening: *What is the relation between government debt levels and real GDP growth?* More sharply: *Is growth lower when central-government debt/GDP is above a threshold around 90%?* Range: 44 countries, up to about 200 years, annual observations, advanced and emerging. What is asked: an association/threshold, though the paper often speaks causally. I freeze it there. Inflation and external debt are secondary.

**2. Jobs and where they came from.**  
J1: Lower median/mean growth above 90% (given).  
J2: A threshold near 90% (fixed by authors).  
J3: Similar public-debt threshold in advanced and emerging (given).  
J4: External-debt threshold around 60% for emerging markets (given).  
J5: No inflation link for advanced; higher inflation for emerging (given).  
J6: Exceptions such as Australia/New Zealand with high debt and strong growth (given).  
J7: Reverse causation—slow growth raising debt/GDP (added by me).

**3. Parts and marks.**

| Part | Mark | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 44-country, 3,700-observation data set | **Borrowed** | Rests on Reinhart-Rogoff data work and many outside sources; not tested here. |
| Four debt buckets, 90% cutoff | **Fixed** | Authors set them; footnote 5 says they are based on interpretation and sensitivity “merits exploration.” |
| Lower growth above 90% | **Held if** | Held by the grouped averages only if the 90/bucket choice is sound. |
| Mean growth several percent lower | **Held if** | Averages can be moved by a few high-debt years; US has only 5 obs above 90%, average -1.8%. |
| Similar threshold advanced/emerging | **Held if** | Similarity is in bucket averages; no shared mechanism is tested. |
| External-debt 60/90 threshold for emerging | **Held if** | Holds for the emerging sample; advanced external thresholds are not tested. |
| No inflation link, advanced | **Unknown** | Negative group result, with US exception; country/period tests would settle it. |
| Inflation rises with debt, emerging | **Held if** | Pattern is in the data; “fiscal dominance” is an interpretation, not measured. |
| Debt intolerance / risk premia | **Borrowed** | From Reinhart-Rogoff-Savastano 2003; not tested here. |
| Barro tax-distortion channel | **Borrowed** | From Barro 1979. |
| Fiscal dominance | **Borrowed** | Asserted as a plausible reading. |
| Private deleveraging slows growth | **Borrowed** | Rests on crisis/deleveraging literature; US figure is an illustration. |
| “Lagged debt should not dramatically change” | **Unknown** | Asserted; the test is not shown. |
| War vs peacetime debt genesis ignored | **Fixed** | Authors state they do not discriminate; not tested. |

**4. Change list.**  
The claim covers changes in debt/GDP across countries and years, advanced vs emerging, public vs external debt, growth and inflation, and long historical periods. It openly leaves out war vs peacetime debt, advanced external-debt thresholds, country-specific thresholds, and cutoff sensitivity. It leaves out more quietly: reverse causation, debt composition (maturity, currency), and the fact that slow growth itself raises debt/GDP by shrinking the denominator.

**5. Tests run.**  
**Remove:** Remove the 90 cutoff and use a continuous debt measure—the sharp threshold may weaken; not shown. Remove inflation—the growth result stands.  
**Swap:** Swap 90 for 80 or 100. Not shown; footnote admits this. Swap median for average: the mean falls much more, suggesting outliers. Swap advanced for emerging: the growth similarity roughly survives, the inflation part breaks.  
**Flip:** If high debt went with higher growth, could the same parts explain it? The empirical buckets would not; “debt intolerance” would have to be reversed. Flip mostly passes.  
**Poke:** Change debt composition (short-term, foreign-currency) should matter; they say so but do not test it against the 90 line. Change inflation should not matter for advanced growth; they show no link. Change growth: slow growth mechanically raises debt/GDP; this should matter and is not ruled out.  
**Reverse:** The main weakness. The paper mostly shows association. The reverse route—slow growth and deficits raising debt/GDP—is not poked. “Lagged debt should not…” is an assertion.  
**Hunt the answer in the starting points:** “Debt intolerance” and the 90% line risk being the conclusion under another name; risk premia are not measured.  
**Add a job:** When debt falls below 90, does growth recover? If not, the threshold is loose. Not tested.  
**Best rival:** Slow growth causes high debt. No change on the list clearly separates this from high debt causing slow growth.  
**Pull:** “High debt lowers growth” pulls against “slow growth raises debt.” Which gives way is not shown.  
**Patches:** “Country-specific thresholds” and “other vulnerabilities” can absorb exceptions without a gauge. Australia/New Zealand are patched by “post-WWII clustering,” but no before/after test is given.  
**Look inside:** The paper mostly matches outputs (growth averages), not workings (why 90%).

**6. Where each part came from.**  
The buckets and averages are **fitted** to past cases. The causal stories—risk premia, taxes, fiscal dominance—are **borrowed** or **asserted**. The 90 cutoff is **fixed**. The lagged-debt claim is **asserted**. The data set is **borrowed**.

**7. What would make it harder to vary.**  
Pre-specify cutoffs and test 80/90/100 and a continuous measure out-of-sample. Poke the reverse direction: use lagged debt/growth, cases where debt rose for reasons unrelated to growth, and see whether growth later falls. Decompose high-debt years by currency, maturity, and war/peace, and show the 90 line survives. The reverse-causation poke and cutoff sensitivity would tighten it most.

**8. What this does not show.**  
Hard to vary is not true. Passing would not prove causality. Failing would not prove the paper false. It can still be a useful warning.

**9. One next step.**  
Run the reverse-causation and cutoff-sensitivity tests before using 90% as a policy trigger.
